summary: This is a theoretical "field synthesis" paper by Garrick Holmes (RIFOR) proposing that two independently established findings—hydration force governance of nanoscale biological lattices (Harrellson et al., 2023) and intrinsic hydrogen bond asymmetry in water (Gunkel et al., 2024)—intersect in the DNA hydration shell. The paper proposes that the DNA minor groove functions as a hydration solid, that molecular bond asymmetry governs shell ordering and exchange dynamics, and that the asymmetric hydration shell is part of DNA's electrical pathway. No original experiments are reported; the paper proposes four future experiments and is explicitly presented as a conceptual synthesis for evaluation by domain experts.

content_blocks.title: Abstract
content_blocks.content: Theoretical proposal connecting two published findings: (1) hygroscopic biological materials as 'hydration solids' governed by hydration force in nanoscale pores (Harrellson et al., 2023), and (2) intrinsic hydrogen bond asymmetry in water—one strong, one weak donor bond, anti-correlated, refreshed sub-picosecond (Gunkel et al., 2024). The paper proposes the DNA hydration shell is a hydration solid, that molecular bond asymmetry determines ordering and exchange dynamics of first-shell water in the minor groove, and that the asymmetric shell is part of DNA's electrical pathway. Four experiments are proposed using existing methods. No original experimental data is presented.

content_blocks.title: Section 1: On Field Synthesis
content_blocks.content: Defines 'field synthesis' as identifying published results across disciplines, recognizing structural connections, and proposing integrated research pathways for domain expert evaluation. The paper explicitly positions itself as a conceptual exercise, not an experimental report. TRL implication: This is a TRL 1 document—basic principles observed and reported, no experimental validation of the proposed mechanism.

content_blocks.title: Section 2: The Hydrated Helix — Background Evidence
content_blocks.content: Summarizes established literature on DNA hydration: (1) DNA requires water to maintain B-form; dehydration causes conformational change. (2) High-resolution crystallography resolves ordered water chain in minor groove ('spine of hydration') with high occupancy. (3) Chiral SFG spectroscopy shows DNA confers handedness on first-shell water, constituting a structured phase distinct from bulk solvent (McDermott et al., 2017; Perets and Yan, 2017; Perets et al., 2024). (4) Drug binding disrupts chiral water structure (Santiago et al., 2025). (5) NMR data: spine water in minor groove resides ~1 ns at 4°C and 10–15 ns at lowest temperatures measured, ~10x longer than major groove water (Halle and Denisov, 1998). All cited evidence is from prior published literature, not original experiments.

content_blocks.title: Section 3: The Hydration Solid Framework
content_blocks.content: Describes Harrellson et al. (2023) framework: hygroscopic biological materials (bacterial spores, pollens, fungal walls) exhibit convergent mechanical behavior governed by hydration force—a short-range repulsive interfacial force dominating transport and elasticity at nanometer-scale pore dimensions. In spore cortex (~4 nm pores), overlapping hydration force fields retard water transport by orders of magnitude beyond conventional prediction. First proposal of the paper: DNA minor groove (nanometric width, bounded by sugar-phosphate backbones with anionic phosphate oxygens and base-edge heteroatoms) satisfies conditions for hydration solid geometry. This is a conceptual proposal, not experimentally tested.

content_blocks.title: Section 4: The Asymmetric Molecule and Proposed Mechanism
content_blocks.content: Describes Gunkel et al. (2024): ultrafast spectroscopy of isotopically dilute water shows two H-bonds donated by a single water molecule are markedly anti-correlated in strength (one strong, one weak), refreshed in <500 femtoseconds. Measurement made in dimethylformamide; not yet tested in pure water. Minor-groove spine water residence (~1 ns at 4°C) is ~3 orders of magnitude longer than the anti-correlation refresh, so asymmetry is a standing property during each residence event. Proposed mechanism: first-shell water donates to chemically inequivalent acceptors (strong anionic phosphate oxygens vs. weaker base-edge heteroatoms). Two proposed consequences: (1) Ordering—strong bond matched to stronger acceptor biases stable occupation of hydration positions; (2) Exchange—mismatched molecules require re-randomization of anti-correlation, adding a step beyond conventional translational/rotational exchange models. All mechanistic claims are proposals, not experimentally validated.

content_blocks.title: Section 5: The Electrical Hydrogen Bond
content_blocks.content: Synthesizes evidence that hydrogen bonds are electrical structures: (1) Compton X-ray scattering on ice shows substantial covalent character with electron sharing (Isaacs et al., 1999). (2) Correlated vibrational spectroscopy in liquid water: hydroxide ions donate ~8% more negative charge to network; hydronium ions accept ~4% less (Flór et al., 2024). (3) Femtosecond spectroscopy: proton shuttles between neighboring oxygens in <100 fs; ≥15 water molecules involved in moving one proton's charge; proton transfer between acid and base runs through H-bonded water wire of 2–4 molecules (Bakker group, AMOLF). DNA electrical data: charge transport through 100 bp DNA (34 nm); single mismatched base pair cuts signal ~in half (ratio 2.3 ± 0.4, Slinker et al., 2011). DNA (414 bp) between gold electrodes: ~10 TΩ at 30% RH, ~250 MΩ at 80–90% RH (drop of ~40,000×, reversible on drying; Tuukkanen et al., 2005). Proposal: asymmetric hydration shell is part of DNA's electrical pathway; mismatch/lesion alters groove, alters shell, alters pathway.

content_blocks.title: Section 6: Proposed Experiments
content_blocks.content:
Four proposed experiments, none yet conducted:

6.1 Isotopic substitution: D2O/H2O substitution; if asymmetric bonding contributes to shell structure, substitution alters first-shell ordering and exchange timescales beyond mass-dependent isotope effect on diffusion (null hypothesis). Detection via chiral SFG spectroscopy (Perets et al., 2024) or nanomechanical measurement of water-exchange timescales in DNA films/DNA-coated cantilevers.

6.2 Counterion and temperature perturbations: Predict systematic shifts in DNA first-shell observables under counterion substitution across alkali series and under temperature scans (modulating anti-correlation lifetime). Reference: ion-specific restructuring of confined H-bond networks in nanochannels (Bi et al., 2026).

6.3 Sequence dependence: AT-rich sequences (narrow minor grooves, coherent acceptor pattern) vs. GC-rich sequences (wider grooves, exocyclic amino group). Detection via chiral SFG or crystallographic water-occupancy comparisons.

6.4 Hydration and charge transport: Measure charge transport through matched/mismatched DNA (as in Slinker et al., 2011) and conductance across relative humidity (as in Tuukkanen et al., 2005) in H2O vs. D2O. Null hypothesis: mass-dependent isotope effect. Signature: excess change in D2O or mismatch effect varying with hydration.

content_blocks.title: Section 7: Outlook
content_blocks.content: Proposes broader applicability: if confirmed at DNA, mechanism applies to other confined-water biological systems. References undocumented relationships between cellular water state, membrane potential, and tissue biomechanics (Cone, 1971; Holmes, 2026). Causal chain proposed: molecule → shell → chromatin → cell. Oncology connection: if shell carries part of DNA's charge, damage disturbing the shell would show electrically. All speculative; no experimental data.

content_blocks.title: DNA Hydration Shell Proposal: Argument Map (Figure, Page 6)
content_blocks.content: Flow diagram showing the logical structure of the paper's argument. Four published findings (top row, solid boxes): Hydration solids (Harrellson 2023), Ordered DNA water (Perets 2024; Halle 1998), Asymmetric H-bonds (Gunkel 2024), Electrical H-bonds (Isaacs 1999; Slinker 2011). These feed into the central proposal (solid box): 'DNA minor groove as a hydration solid.' This generates three consequences (solid boxes): Ordering (strong-weak matches sites), Exchange (extra re-randomization step), Electrical pathway (shell chains carry charge). Four proposed experiments (dashed boxes): D2O/H2O + SFG, Ions + temperature, AT vs GC grooves, Charge transport H2O vs D2O. Outlook (dashed box): Cell water, chromatin, DNA damage. Legend distinguishes published findings, this paper's proposals, and extensions.

content_blocks.title: Section 8: Conclusion and References
content_blocks.content: Concludes that two established findings (hydration force governance and H-bond asymmetry) have not previously intersected; proposes they meet in the DNA hydration shell. Specifies mechanism, proposes shell as part of DNA's electrical pathway, and proposes four experiments. References include: Bakker group AMOLF (proton conduction); Bi et al. 2026 (Nature Communications, not yet confirmed); Cone 1971; Flór et al. 2024 (Science); Gunkel et al. 2024 (Nature Communications); Halle & Denisov 1998 (Biopolymers); Harrellson et al. 2023 (Nature); Holmes 2026 (Inventum Biologicum); Isaacs et al. 1999 (PRL); McDermott et al. 2017 (ACS Central Science); Perets & Yan 2017 (ACS Central Science); Perets et al. 2024 (J. Chem. Phys.); Santiago et al. 2025 (Chemical Science); Slinker et al. 2011 (Nature Chemistry); Tuukkanen et al. 2005 (Applied Physics Letters).

key_findings: This is a purely theoretical 'field synthesis' paper with no original experimental data; TRL is 1 (basic principles observed and reported, conceptual proposal only).

Core proposal: DNA minor groove qualifies as a 'hydration solid' (Harrellson et al., 2023 framework), and intrinsic water H-bond asymmetry (Gunkel et al., 2024) governs ordering and exchange dynamics of first-shell water.

Proposed mechanism: water molecules in the minor groove donate one strong bond to anionic phosphate oxygens and one weak bond to base-edge heteroatoms; matched orientation stabilizes hydration positions; mismatched orientation requires additional re-randomization step for exchange.
Second proposal: the asymmetric hydration shell is part of DNA's electrical pathway, linking shell structure to DNA conductance and the electrical signature of DNA damage/mismatches.

Supporting literature cited (not original): DNA conductance drops ~40,000× from 30% to 80–90% RH (Tuukkanen et al., 2005); single base-pair mismatch cuts charge transport signal by ~half (ratio 2.3 ± 0.4, Slinker et al., 2011).

Minor groove spine water residence time ~1 ns at 4°C (NMR, Halle & Denisov 1998), ~3 orders of magnitude longer than H-bond asymmetry refresh (<500 fs), making asymmetry a standing property during residence.

Four experiments proposed (none conducted): (1) D2O/H2O isotopic substitution + chiral SFG; (2) counterion/temperature perturbations; (3) sequence-dependent (AT vs GC) shell observables; (4) charge transport in H2O vs D2O.

Author is affiliated with 'RIFOR' (independent research organization); paper is explicitly self-described as a conceptual exercise for evaluation by domain experts, not a report of completed experiments.
One cited reference (Bi et al., 2026) is explicitly flagged as 'not yet confirmed' in the reference list, raising questions about citation reliability.
Holmes (2026) is self-cited, suggesting this is part of a broader personal research program.
